key_insight: Treating severity classification as a probing benchmark reveals how well small language models — including those augmented for chain-of-thought or reasoning — actually interpret system log semantics and runtime behaviors, not just map labels to text. The paper benchmarks these small models to surface differences in reliability, calibration, and generalization.
problem_solved: Provides a focused evaluation framework to assess whether compact LMs truly understand and reason about system logs (beyond label memorization), enabling practical selection and improvement of lightweight log analysis models.
method: Construct a severity-classification benchmark from real system logs and define probing scenarios (in-distribution, out-of-distribution, noisy/partial logs).
Compare small baseline LMs against small reasoning-augmented variants using standard metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness) and explanatory probes.
Analyze failures and calibration to identify whether errors come from surface cues, lack of runtime reasoning, or dataset artifacts.
impact: Helps ML engineers and SREs choose and tune compact models for log monitoring pipelines while understanding trade-offs between model size, reasoning capability, and trustworthiness. Encourages evaluation practices that probe true interpretive ability rather than label prediction.
visual_elements: Bar chart comparing accuracy and calibration error for small LMs vs small reasoning LMs across test splits
Confusion matrices or stacked bars showing common misclassification patterns (e.g., INFO vs WARNING vs ERROR)
Pipeline diagram: raw logs → preprocessing → model types (baseline vs reasoning) → metrics + explanation probe
Annotated example log message showing model prediction, confidence score, and short chain-of-thought explanation
paper_title: Benchmarking Small Language Models and Small Reasoning Language Models on System Log Severity Classification
paper_authors: Yahya Masri, Emily Ma, Zifu Wang, Joseph Rogers, Chaowei Yang
